This append is an additional, explicitly recorded provenance change in the parent amendment stage; it is not silently included in changedFields here.

applicationContract.reviewDateRule: provenance.lastReviewed, provenance.upstreamRevision and automation.validatedAt remain unchanged/null. Source document revisions below are not a human review or an upstream recommendation mapping.
applicationContract.hashRule: beforeFileSha256 fingerprints actual UTF-8 file bytes; beforeDocumentSha256 and proposedFieldsDocumentSha256 use canonical JSON sorted keys, compact separators, ensure_ascii=false, UTF-8. proposedFieldsDocumentSha256 includes only the exact listed field replacements, before the separately required provenance.sources append. These are local document/precondition hashes, not hashes of upstream recommendations.
applicationContract.historyRule: Apply only through a new semantic amendment stage after the completed service-normalization stage. Existing pillar and normalization reports must remain historical; test replay must verify/reverse the new stage before earlier-stage replay. Do not weaken original guidance/identity/query assertions.
applicationContract.reviewImpact: Every proposed applied change is semantic guidance and/or applicability curation, not an alias/case normalization. Pinned review snapshots remain unchanged until an explicit review refresh.

A later approved catalogue change should recognize it as a legacy Data Factory type alongside factories without making the types semantic aliases. The current policy-only mapping would otherwise report a false contradiction for explicit WAF service classifications on logging hosts. Preserve SKU and WAF-enabled caveats; do not infer every CDN profile is a Front Door WAF.

sources.title: Azure permissions for Analytics - Azure RBAC
sources.readingScope: Microsoft.DataFactory table, including parent datafactories operations and legacy slices/gateways versus factories and integrationruntimes.
findings: The current Microsoft-generated permissions reference explicitly lists Microsoft.DataFactory/datafactories/read, write and delete; the spelling therefore cannot be dismissed as a nonexistent typo.
The same table separately lists factories and its integrationruntimes, triggers and managedVirtualNetworks. These are different resource scopes, not casing variants.
A current permissions listing alone does not establish current provisioning availability, support lifecycle, or that a v2-specific recommendation applies to v1.

sources.title: Tutorial: Migrate your V1 Azure Data Factory to V2
sources.readingScope: Complete Microsoft-owned migration tutorial; explicit v1/v2 distinction and preview/manual conversion of datasets, linked services and pipelines.
findings: The official sample repository treats v1-to-v2 as a migration that can require manual conversion, not a resource-type spelling fix.
The tree identifier pins the fetched file; it is not asserted to be a recommendation identity or a commit ID.

sources.title: Microsoft.DataFactory/factories - Bicep, ARM template & Terraform AzAPI reference
sources.readingScope: V2-labelled Bicep sample, factories@2018-06-01 resource format, identity and repoConfiguration properties.
findings: The reference explicitly labels the factories@2018-06-01 example as Data Factory Version 2 and includes Git repository configuration.

sources.title: Source control - Azure Data Factory
sources.readingScope: Introduction, Git integration benefits, repository configuration and explicit warning about changes made outside Git.
findings: Git stores factory entity JSON and supports versioning, collaboration and deployment workflows; direct PowerShell/SDK changes are not automatically entered into Git.
The service authoring experience is not a backup of all dependencies or moved data. An ARM template for the factory itself needs separate attention.

sources.title: Reliability in Azure Data Factory
sources.readingScope: Complete article: architecture, IR-specific zone redundancy, trigger-state caveats, region failover, SHIR responsibilities, custom recovery, backup and SLA.
findings: The core service and Azure IR have Microsoft-managed zone redundancy. Azure-SSIS requires two or more nodes; SHIR compute resilience is customer-managed.
Tumbling-window trigger state has a zone-failure caveat. Pipelines/activities should support safe retries; zone redundancy is not a single customer pipeline switch.
Microsoft-managed regional failover is conditional, best effort and potentially delayed, with region exceptions. Custom recovery and restored networking can be necessary.
SHIR compute recovery remains the customer's responsibility; Azure Site Recovery is one documented option for an SHIR on Azure VMs.
CI/CD and source control protect deployable factory metadata, not the complete workload's data and dependencies.

sources.title: Secure your Azure Data Factory deployment - Azure Data Factory
sources.readingScope: Redirect destination; network/identity dependencies and Backup and recovery section.
findings: The old architecture link now redirects; it must not be cited as though the historical article was retrieved unchanged.
Current guidance places Git integration on development factories and uses CI/CD to promote to test/production.
Network, secret and identity dependencies need explicit treatment; deployment templates provide a deployable configuration backup.

sources.title: Store credentials in Azure Key Vault - Azure Data Factory
sources.readingScope: Complete article: runtime credential retrieval, managed identity prerequisite, linked service and secret version references.
findings: The documented integration retrieves referenced credentials at activity execution and depends on factory identity, vault access and reachable endpoints.
This supports a dependency-specific availability review; it does not prove an SLA for the combined pipeline or remove customer recovery responsibilities.

sources.title: Reliability in Azure Key Vault
sources.readingScope: Architecture, regional pairing exceptions, transient fault handling, automatic zonal redundancy and managed regional failover limitations.
findings: Zone redundancy is automatic where supported, but cross-region replication/failover has regional exceptions.
Microsoft-managed regional failover can be delayed, is best effort and can leave the vault read-only. Critical workloads may need custom multiregion recovery.
The legacy statement that an ADF user need do nothing about Key Vault replication/recovery is too unconditional.

sources.title: Microsoft.Network/FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallPolicies - Bicep, ARM template & Terraform AzAPI reference
sources.readingScope: Resource format, resource type, SKU description and tier-specific usage examples.
findings: The documented policy resource is Microsoft.Network/FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallPolicies.
The current reference describes Classic as the default policy SKU when none is specified and includes Standard/Premium examples; the type alone does not identify a Front Door tier.
Do not substitute this policy type for every logging host or every regional reverse proxy.

sources.title: Microsoft.Network/FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallPolicies 2018-08-01 - Bicep, ARM template & Terraform AzAPI reference
sources.readingScope: Version-specific 2018-08-01 Resource format, not the generic modern sample reused above it.
findings: The oldest version linked by the current reference also uses FrontDoorWebApplicationFirewallPolicies.
No fetched primary source establishes frontdoorwebapplicationfirewalls as an older equivalent resource type. Absence from this bounded evidence is not proof that it never existed.

sources.title: Monitoring and Logging - Azure Web Application Firewall
sources.readingScope: Complete article including distinct Standard/Premium and classic diagnostic examples.
findings: WAF logs are not enabled by default; diagnostic settings are configured on the Front Door resource.
Standard/Premium examples identify Microsoft.Cdn/Profiles while classic examples identify FRONTDOORS under Microsoft.Network.
The rule log categories differ in capitalization by tier. No proposed KQL is generated from these examples.

sources.title: Best practices for Azure Web Application Firewall in Azure Front Door
sources.readingScope: Complete article, especially logging and Microsoft Sentinel sections; current Applies to label.
findings: The current best-practices article is labelled Front Door Premium; it cannot alone justify identical capabilities on Standard or classic.
It recommends retained logs for false-positive/attack review and importing WAF telemetry into Sentinel or another SIEM.

sources.title: Using Microsoft Sentinel with Azure Web Application Firewall
sources.readingScope: Complete article: resource-specific diagnostics, WAF solution/connector and detection rules.
findings: Front Door and Application Gateway diagnostic data can be sent to the Log Analytics workspace used by the Sentinel WAF solution/connector.

The article covers distinct classic and Standard/Premium hosts. Exact category labels differ from the dedicated current WAF logging article; choose categories exposed by the actual resource rather than copying conflicting snippets.

sources.title: What Is Azure Web Application Firewall on Azure Front Door?
sources.readingScope: Global edge architecture, applicability labels and tier capabilities; no proposal relies on newly described attachment-scope behavior.
findings: Front Door WAF is a global edge service, not a proxy deployed inside a customer's landing-zone virtual network.
Front Door Standard supports custom rules; Premium has managed-rule capabilities. Policy type and generic CDN profile type alone do not encode this distinction.

sources.title: Secure traffic to origins - Azure Front Door
sources.readingScope: Tier support table, public origin IP/header combination, Application Gateway example and classic retirement notice.
findings: Public origins should combine AzureFrontDoor.Backend source filtering with validation of their own Front Door identifier; shared source IPs alone are insufficient.
Application Gateway guidance uses NSG filtering and a WAF custom rule for the X-Azure-FDID header.
Private Link is a Premium-specific option, not a requirement universally applicable to Standard/classic or every origin.
Classic retires March 31, 2027; existing classic deployments are not silently omitted by the proposals.

sources.title: What Is Azure Web Application Firewall on Azure Application Gateway?
sources.readingScope: Application Gateway-specific WAF architecture, monitoring, policy associations and logging.
findings: Application Gateway WAF is a distinct regional application-delivery surface, with diagnostic logs on Application Gateway.
The article distinguishes WAF_v1/WAF_v2 and states policy associations are supported only for WAF_v2; blanket conversion to a Front Door policy type is incorrect.

sources.title: Plan for inbound and outbound internet connectivity - Cloud Adoption Framework
sources.readingScope: Inbound HTTP/S design recommendations only; unrelated outbound/firewall recommendations were not imported.
findings: The page separately recommends regional WAF/partner NVAs in the application landing-zone network and global protection using Front Door WAF.
It explicitly recommends origin restriction when Front Door and Application Gateway are combined.
The distinction resolves the imported landing-zone proxy record's incorrect Front Door-type association without asserting that every partner proxy runs on a particular ARM compute type.

sources.title: Best practices for reliability - Azure Databricks
sources.readingScope: Design for failure / resilient distributed engine; compared separate job-retry and Structured Streaming recovery sections.
findings: The imported description matches the resilient distributed-engine section: Spark reschedules missing/failed tasks after some infrastructure faults, including brief network interruptions or a revoked Spot VM.
The section separately describes Photon as a high-performance Spark-API-compatible engine; it does not prescribe Photon as the switch enabling Spark fault recovery.
Job retry/termination and streaming checkpoint recovery are separate recommendations, not equivalent requirements.
Other unreviewed sections on this long page are not adopted or treated as independently verified; this pass does not validate all Databricks availability claims.

sources.title: What is Photon? - Azure Databricks
sources.readingScope: Complete article: execution model, enablement and limitations.
findings: Photon accelerates supported SQL/DataFrame execution and falls back for unsupported operations; this is a performance capability, not the source of Spark task-recovery semantics.
Not all APIs/workloads benefit or are supported. The reconciliation does not convert this reliability requirement into a blanket Photon enablement recommendation.

records.name: revcl-AdfPipelinesKeyVault

Key Vault provides managed redundancy, but cross-region replication and Microsoft-managed failover have regional exceptions and can be delayed; they do not guarantee coordinated recovery with Data Factory. records.name: revcl-SelfHostedIntegrationRuntimeVmsRegion

records.name: revcl-SisterRegionNetwork

before.title: Make sure you replicate or duplicate your network in the sister region. You have to make a copy of your Vnet in another region

after.title: Recreate required Data Factory v2 connectivity in the selected recovery region
after.description: For a Data Factory v2 regional recovery design, document and recreate the networking needed by the selected integration runtimes and data dependencies, including applicable virtual networks, routes, name resolution and private connectivity. Validate connectivity to recovered data stores, Key Vault and SHIR hosts. Select the recovery region according to recovery objectives, service support and data-residency constraints; do not assume every factory has an appropriate paired region or that duplicating a virtual network alone restores pipeline operation.

records.reason: Current regional-recovery guidance requires restoring networking but distinguishes paired/nonpaired regions and customer requirements. Preserve the dependency objective while explicitly maintaining it for v2, rather than pretending 'sister region' is universal.

records.name: revcl-ZoneRedundantPipelinesAvailabilityZones

before.title: Use zone redundant pipelines in regions that support Availability Zones

after.title: Verify component-specific zone resilience for Data Factory v2 pipelines and integration runtimes
after.description: In regions that support availability zones, the Data Factory core service and Azure integration runtime provide Microsoft-managed zone redundancy without a pipeline setting. For Azure-SSIS IR, use at least two nodes for automatic distribution across zones; for SHIR, provide customer-managed resilient compute across zones. Account for dependent data stores and the documented tumbling-window trigger-state caveat, and design retried activities to be idempotent. Do not interpret a factory's region alone as proof that every pipeline dependency is zone-resilient.

records.reason: Correct an implied universal 'zone redundant pipeline' toggle by explaining documented per-component responsibilities within an explicit v2 applicability amendment.
limitations: No Azure configuration, regional availability or failover was executed/verified live.
Existing high severity and Reliability pillar are retained, not recalculated.

Review ingestion and detection coverage rather than assuming that forwarding logs alone provides complete attack detection. Diagnostics belong to the application delivery resource: Front Door Standard/Premium uses Microsoft.Cdn/profiles with an Azure Front Door SKU, classic uses Microsoft.Network/frontdoors, and Application Gateway uses Microsoft.Network/applicationGateways. Other CDN profile SKUs are not implicitly in scope.

Application Gateway diagnostics use Microsoft.Network/applicationGateways.
